task_1.title: Fix child module attributes missing on parent modules under --import-mode=importlib
task_1.description: When pytest runs with --import-mode=importlib, it generates intermediate (fake) modules to make dotted imports work. However, these intermediate modules did not register child modules as attributes on their parent modules. This caused an AttributeError when test code accessed a child module via dotted attribute notation on the parent (e.g., parent_pkg.child_mod.func()), even though importing the child directly (from parent_pkg import child_mod) still worked. The fix ensures that as the module hierarchy is walked, each child module is set as an attribute on its parent, restoring standard Python module attribute semantics.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that when pytest operates under --import-mode=importlib, intermediate modules created for the import hierarchy correctly expose child modules as attributes of their parent modules. Previously, accessing a child module through dotted attribute access on a parent package (e.g., `parent_package.child_module`) raised an AttributeError, even though direct import of the child succeeded. This regression was introduced when doctest support began respecting import-mode=importlib.

expectation.grounded: The `insert_missing_modules` function in the pathlib module must, while walking up the module name hierarchy, set each child module as an attribute on its parent module via setattr if the parent does not already have that attribute. Both newly created dummy modules and modules already present in sys.modules must have their child attributes populated. After the function completes, for any module name 'a.b.c', the module object for 'a.b' must have attribute 'c' referencing the module for 'a.b.c', and 'a' must have attribute 'b' referencing the module for 'a.b'.
expectation.conceptual: When pytest uses importlib import mode, all intermediate package modules in the import hierarchy must expose their direct child modules as attributes. Dotted attribute access (e.g., `pkg.submodule.function()`) must work identically to explicit imports (`from pkg import submodule`). The behavior must match standard Python import semantics where child modules are always accessible as attributes of their parent packages.

constraints.grounded: Child module attributes must only be set on the parent if the parent does not already have an attribute with that name (i.e., existing attributes must not be overwritten). The fix must apply to both fake/dummy modules created by pytest and real modules already present in sys.modules. The fix must not alter behavior when --import-mode is not set to importlib. The modules dict passed to insert_missing_modules must remain consistent with the attribute relationships established.
constraints.conceptual: Existing module attributes must never be overwritten by this fix. The change must be scoped to importlib import mode only and must not affect default or prepend import modes. Both real and synthetic intermediate modules must be handled uniformly. Standard Python module attribute resolution semantics must be preserved.

behavior: When insert_missing_modules processes a dotted module name, it now tracks the most recently processed child module and its short name as it walks up the hierarchy from leaf to root.

For each parent module encountered (whether newly created, freshly imported, or already registered), the child module is set as an attribute on the parent if no attribute with that name already exists.

Modules already present in sys.modules (not just newly created dummy modules) now also receive child attribute assignment, closing the gap where real parent modules lacked references to pytest-imported children.
After processing, dotted attribute access like parent_pkg.child_mod resolves correctly instead of raising AttributeError.
The fix preserves idempotency: if a parent already has the child attribute set, it is not overwritten.
acceptance_criteria: Given a package hierarchy (e.g., pkg/__init__.py and pkg/temp.py) and pytest running with --import-mode=importlib, when a test imports the parent package and accesses a child module via dotted attribute (e.g., pkg.temp.func()), then the access should succeed without AttributeError.

Given a package hierarchy with multiple nesting levels (e.g., a.b.c), when pytest runs with --import-mode=importlib and creates intermediate modules, then a.b should have attribute 'c' and a should have attribute 'b'.
Given a parent module that already has a child attribute set (e.g., via __init__.py import), when insert_missing_modules runs, then the existing attribute must not be overwritten.

Given pytest running with --import-mode=importlib and --doctest-modules enabled, when tests and doctests both exist in a package, then tests accessing parent_package.child_module should pass without errors.
Given pytest running without --import-mode=importlib (default or prepend mode), when the same test suite runs, then behavior should remain unchanged from prior versions.

task_3.title: Fix duplicate module imports under importlib import mode
task_3.description: When using --import-mode=importlib together with --doctest-modules, modules could be imported more than once, resulting in multiple distinct module objects for the same module. This caused failures for modules with import side effects (e.g., setting class variables or registering handlers) because the side effects applied to one module instance would not be visible through the other. The fix ensures that the import_path function checks sys.modules for an already-imported module before attempting to import it again, returning the cached instance if present.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that when pytest is configured with --import-mode=importlib, each module is imported exactly once, even when combined with --doctest-modules or other features that trigger multiple import_path calls for the same module. Previously, duplicate imports produced distinct module objects, causing modules with import side effects (e.g., class variable assignments, global state initialization) to appear uninitialized or inconsistent when accessed through a different reference than the one that ran the side effect.

expectation.grounded: When import_path is called with ImportMode.importlib, it should resolve the module name via module_name_from_path and check sys.modules for an existing entry before proceeding with a fresh import. If the module is already present in sys.modules, import_path must return that existing module object. The identity check 'sys.modules[module_name] is <returned module>' must hold true for any subsequent import_path call targeting the same module.
expectation.conceptual: Under importlib import mode, repeated requests to import the same module must always return the same module object. The framework should never create a second, distinct copy of a module that has already been imported. Any global state or side effects established during the first import must be visible through all references to that module.

constraints.grounded: The sys.modules lookup must be performed after module_name_from_path resolves the name but before any meta_path finder or spec-based import is attempted. A missing key in sys.modules (KeyError) must be silently suppressed so that first-time imports proceed through the normal importlib discovery path. The fix must not alter behavior for ImportMode.prepend or ImportMode.append modes. Modules that have never been imported must still go through the full importlib import machinery.
constraints.conceptual: The deduplication check must only apply to the importlib import mode and must not interfere with the first-time import path. Other import modes must remain unaffected. The solution must gracefully handle the case where the module has not yet been imported without raising errors.

behavior: When import_path is invoked with ImportMode.importlib for a module already present in sys.modules, the cached module object from sys.modules is returned immediately without re-executing the module's import machinery.
When import_path is invoked with ImportMode.importlib for a module not yet in sys.modules, the full importlib-based discovery and import proceeds as before.
Using --import-mode=importlib together with --doctest-modules no longer causes the same module to appear as two distinct objects in the process.
Module-level side effects (class variable assignments, global registrations, singleton initialization) are executed exactly once and are visible through all references to that module.
acceptance_criteria: When running pytest with --import-mode=importlib and --doctest-modules on a project where a test module imports a library module, the library module object accessible in the test must be identical (by identity) to the one in sys.modules.

Given a module that sets a class variable as an import side effect, when pytest imports that module via importlib mode and a test references the module, then the class variable must be present and reflect the side effect.
When a module is imported for the first time under importlib mode, it should go through the standard importlib finder/spec path and be added to sys.modules normally.
When import_path is called multiple times for the same module path under importlib mode, sys.modules must contain exactly one entry for that module name, and all calls must return the same object.
Existing behavior under --import-mode=prepend and --import-mode=append must remain unchanged by this fix.

task_2.title: Fix pytest.approx TypeError when comparing dictionaries containing None values
task_2.description: When using pytest.approx() to compare dictionaries where either the expected or actual value for a key is None, the assertion error representation would crash with a TypeError ('unsupported operand type(s) for -: float and NoneType') instead of producing a clear AssertionError showing which keys differ. The fix guards the numeric difference calculation so that None values are handled gracefully, allowing the assertion to fail with a properly formatted error message.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that pytest.approx() correctly handles None values when comparing dictionaries. Previously, when an expected or actual dictionary value was None, the assertion failure representation crashed with a TypeError instead of producing a readable assertion error. After the fix, pytest.approx() should gracefully skip numeric difference computation for None values and report the differing keys in the standard assertion error format.

expectation.grounded: When pytest.approx() compares two dictionaries and a mismatched pair contains None on either the expected or actual side, the ApproxMapping comparison logic should skip the absolute and relative difference calculations for that pair. The key should still be identified as different and included in the assertion error output. No TypeError should be raised during the error representation. The max_abs_diff and max_rel_diff values should only be updated for pairs where both values are non-None numeric types.
expectation.conceptual: When pytest.approx() encounters None values in dictionary comparisons, it should produce a clean, readable assertion error that identifies which keys differ, rather than crashing with a TypeError. The comparison should treat None as a legitimately different value without attempting arithmetic on it.

constraints.grounded: The fix must not alter the behavior of pytest.approx() when all dictionary values are numeric (non-None). The absolute and relative difference statistics must still be correctly computed for all non-None mismatched pairs. Keys with None values must still appear in the list of differing keys reported in the assertion error. The fix must handle both cases: when the expected value is None and the actual is numeric, and when the actual value is None and the expected is numeric.
constraints.conceptual: Existing numeric dictionary comparisons via pytest.approx() must continue to work identically. The fix must only change behavior in the presence of None values. Both directions of None mismatch (None vs float and float vs None) must be handled consistently.

behavior: When pytest.approx(expected_dict) == actual_dict is evaluated and a key has None as the expected value but a numeric actual value, the comparison no longer raises TypeError during assertion error formatting.

When pytest.approx(expected_dict) == actual_dict is evaluated and a key has a numeric expected value but None as the actual value, the comparison no longer raises TypeError during assertion error formatting.
Keys whose values involve None are still correctly identified as differing and included in the assertion error message.
The max absolute difference and max relative difference statistics are only computed across pairs where both values are non-None, preventing arithmetic on None.
For fully numeric dictionary comparisons, behavior is unchanged from the previous version.
acceptance_criteria: When comparing pytest.approx({'a': None}) against {'a': 1.2}, an AssertionError is raised with a readable message identifying key 'a' as different, and no TypeError occurs.
When comparing pytest.approx({'a': 1.2}) against {'a': None}, an AssertionError is raised with a readable message identifying key 'a' as different, and no TypeError occurs.
When comparing pytest.approx({'a': 1.0, 'b': None}) against {'a': 1.0, 'b': 2.0}, only key 'b' is reported as different, and no TypeError occurs.
When comparing pytest.approx({'a': 1.0, 'b': 2.0}) against {'a': 1.0, 'b': 2.0000001}, existing approximate equality behavior is preserved and the assertion passes.

When comparing pytest.approx({'a': 1.0, 'b': 3.0}) against {'a': 1.0, 'b': 5.0}, the assertion error correctly reports absolute and relative differences for the numeric mismatch, unchanged from prior behavior.
